C. Impact on Community Services
One frequent reason given for resistance by a community to new housing developments is that community services will require extensive and expensive expansion, particularly in the areas of education, police protection, and sanitary sewage system additions. In every case, the planners and HUD discussed all such potential problems with the local community officials in order to identify actual problem areas. Where appropriate, water, sewer and open space grants were processed to provide assistance to the community to meet these additional costs. As noted, the Jersey City site development will include a school so as to supplement an existing overcrowded school situation. Finally, all of the sites will generate tax revenue to the local communities.
D. Potential Impact on Property Values
Another potential obstacle to housing development, and particularly the development of housing intended in part for lower income people of a different ethnic or racial background, is the belief that this will bring down adjacent property values. This type of resistance was found on several sites in varying degree. Extensive efforts were made by the site planners and HUD Washington and Regional staff to explain the program, to describe the type of development, and to provide factual information countering the rumors which were found to be the basis for opposition. It is the belief of the Department that the BREAK-THROUGH sites will prove to enhance, and not destroy, the property values of the surrounding community.
4. ALTERNATIVES TO THE PROPOSED ACTION
A. No Program
This theoretical alternative was never seriously considered. The housing problem facing the Nation is too critical to back away from any significant opportunity to find a solution.
B. Program Directed Only at Housing Technology
One alternative actively considered was to limit the program to the development of new housing technologies. However no purely technological program which avoided the issue of constraints to innovation could hope to be successful, and the technology thus developed would have little chance for implementation on a wide scale.
C. Different Number and Character of Demonstration Sites
Considerations were given in the program plan development to the kinds and types of demonstration sites to be used, from a "housing fair" approach with one each of a number of housing systems to sites only on Federal land. It was considered necessary, however, to demonstrate both housing and community development, in a wide range of development situations. As noted, the specific sites were selected in a national competition to obtain those which best fit the program plan.
